newsitem.title: FINLAND: Metra sees growth in gas power plants.
newsitem.headline: Metra sees growth in gas power plants.

text.p: Finnish engineering group Metra Oy Ab is expecting its gas-fuelled power plant business to outpace its traditional diesel oil power plant arm as demand for natural gas expands along with supply.

"Our biggest business today is in heavy fuel oil plants, but the fastest growth is in natural gas-fuelled plants," Pentti-Juhani Hintikka, president of Metra's engine-building Wartsila Diesel unit told Reuters by telephone.

Diesel engine and power plant maker Wartsila Diesel is Metra's biggest division. The 1996 merger of Wartsila Diesel and Swiss New Sulzer Diesel will raise its share of Metra group sales close to 80 percent from 65 percent in 1995.
"We see it very much as an opportunity that gas demand is increasing," Metra President and CEO Georg Ehrnrooth told Reuters in an interview late last week.

"In five to 10 years, if environmental concerns continue to develop as they have recently and if gas delivery systems continue to develop as planned, gas-related sales could represent 50 percent of our power plant sales," Ehrnrooth said.
"If you look at what fuel is taking more market share in power production, it is clearly natural gas," Hintikka said.
Gas-related businesses now account for about 15 percent of Wartsila Diesel's power plant business, he said.

"The gas-fuelled small-engine market is already bigger than the heavy fuel oil-fired plant market, and as we already have a high share of the heavy fuel plant business, it will certainly be easier for us to increase our share of the gas-fuelled business," Hintikka said.
Last year, Wartsila Diesel increased its worldwide share of the market for reciprocating engine (diesel, gas and dual-fuel) power plants of over one megawatts to 19 percent from 18 percent.
"If you want to be a credible competitor ... you need 20 to 30 percent market share," Hintikka said.
"We are close to that in our heavy fuel engine business, but with less than 10 percent of the gas engine market we have quite a lot of work to do there," he added.

Because of daily fluctuations and seasonal changes in energy demand, Europe in particular needs regulating power -- that means load management and prime power installations -- which are Wartsila Diesel's main business areas, Hintikka said.
The company sees good sales growth prospects for smaller community power installations generating both heat and electricity.
It also sees growth prospects in a trend towards more small gas-fuelled power plants in distrubuted power systems in Europe.
"There is typically a growth trend (towards) ... decentralised power systems," said Sven Bertlin, president of Wartsila Diesel's Finnish subsidiary Wartsila Diesel Oy.
"It is like the computer industry, where first there were only mainframes and now, in addition to mainframes, you have lots of personal computers as well," Ehrnrooth said.
Wartsila Diesel is also a supplier of engine-driven gas-pumping equipment for pipelines and offshore oil and gas drilling.
"I suppose we could realistically expect to take a 20 to 30 percent market share (and) we should be able to do it in four to five years at the latest," Hintikka said.
Information on Wartsila Diesel's current market share in this segment was not available.

While Metra sees big projects to develop European gas distribution networks creating growth opportunities for its engine and gas-pumping equipment sales, it says Asia will remain the fastest-growing market for its energy-related business.
"Asia will continue to be the biggest growth market, but Europe is becoming more interesting (than before)," Ehrnrooth said.
In 1995, more than 50 percent of Wartsila Diesel's invoiced sales came from Asia.
